Opposition demonstrations were held in Azerbaijan on 2 April 2011.
According to the applicants, the relevant authorities were notified about the demonstrations but refused to authorise them.
Despite their peaceful character, demonstrations held without authorisation were dispersed by the police.
According to the applicants, they had intended to attend the demonstration scheduled for 2 April 2011.
According to the applicants, the first applicant was involved in the organisation of the demonstration scheduled for 2 April 2011.
Prior notice of the demonstration of 2 April 2011 had been given to the relevant authority, the Baku City Executive Authority.
According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the protests planned for 2 April 2011 were organised by Azerbaijan's opposition parties and young social network users.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, ahead of the 2 April protest organised by opposition political parties through Facebook, the Azerbaijani authorities detained at least 11 prominent political activists on 31 March 2011.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, Azerbaijani authorities detained at least 10 opposition activists in an effort to prevent a public rally planned for 2 April 2011 in Baku.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the activists were quickly convicted in summary trials on charges of disobeying police orders and sentenced to administrative detention ranging from five to thirteen days, which would keep them locked up beyond the protest date.

One of the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's recommendations to the Azerbaijani authorities was to end practices of unjustified or selective criminal prosecution of journalists or others who may express critical opinions.

According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's document CommDH(2011)33 of 29 September 2011, the Commissioner's attention was drawn to the wave of arrests of activists and political opponents in connection with protests held in Baku in March and April 2011.

According to the report CommDH(2013)14 of 6 August 2013, the issue of limitations imposed on freedom of assembly has regularly been raised by local and international observers in recent years, with the most frequent problems including the banning of demonstrations in central and easily accessible locations and the use of force to disperse demonstrations, leading to arrests and in some cases harsh sentences.

Resolution 1917 (2013) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe stated that the combination of the restrictive implementation of freedoms with unfair trials and the undue influence of the executive results in the systemic detention of people who may be considered prisoners of conscience in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan (P7_TA(2011)0243) noted that a wide-ranging clampdown on freedom of expression and assembly was being carried out in Azerbaijan following the peaceful protests against the government on 11 March and 2 April 2011.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan noted that the clampdown included arrests, harassment and intimidation of civil society activists, media professionals and opposition politicians in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan strongly deplored the practice of intimidating, arresting, prosecuting and convicting independent journalists and political activists on various criminal charges in Azerbaijan.

The European Parliament Resolution of 12 May 2011 on Azerbaijan encouraged the Azerbaijani authorities to allow peaceful demonstrations to take place in relevant locations and urged them to refrain from intimidating the organisers by detaining them and charging them with criminal and other offences.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, Ilham Huseynli, Nemat Aliyev, Tabriz Qasimov and Mehdi Mehdiyev were given sentences ranging between five and seven days' administrative detention, convicted of resisting police or disturbing the public order despite the fact that the protests had yet to take place.

According to the Amnesty International public statement EUR55/003/2011 of 31 March 2011, the call for protests on 2 April 2011 met with a new wave of violence and intimidation directed against activists and journalists.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 1 April 2011, the activists were quickly convicted in summary trials on charges of disobeying police orders and sentenced to administrative detention ranging from five to thirteen days, which would keep them locked up beyond the protest date.

According to the Amnesty International press release of 2 April 2011, John Dalhuisen stated that the fact that key organisers were being arrested in advance and sentenced in closed trials of offences that had yet to take place was indicative of the length to which the authorities were prepared to go to silence dissenting voices.

According to the Human Rights Watch news release of 12 March 2011, in at least three cases the Azerbaijani authorities held activists on administrative charges just long enough to prevent them from participating in the planned protests.

According to the Contact online news release of 31 March 2011, in connection with the Ictimai Palata's decision to hold the protest at the Fountains Square on 2 April 2011, arrests of potential activists began.
